headline_en: How expatriate Bangladeshis observe Ramadan fasting in South Korea
summary_en: A reader-contributed piece by the president of the Korea-Bangla Press Club describes how Bangladeshi workers in South Korea fast during Ramadan while working normal factory hours, with no reduced working hours, no iftar for sale outside, and constant attention to halal food. It gives figures for Bangladeshis, mosques and Muslims in South Korea.

facts.statement: More than about 30,000 Bangladeshi migrants currently live in South Korea, according to the writer (the article states this figure twice).
facts.source_in_article: Mohammad Hanif, President, Korea-Bangla Press Club (writer)

facts.statement: In South Korea, being a non-Muslim country, migrant workers get no concession of any kind for Ramadan: Muslim workers fast alongside the fixed factory working hours. By contrast the article says Middle Eastern countries including Saudi Arabia, Oman, Kuwait, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain reduce working hours for Ramadan.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammad Hanif, President, Korea-Bangla Press Club (writer)

facts.statement: Bangladeshi workers in South Korea have to take sehri and iftar in gaps during work; on working days most break the fast hurriedly with dates and water after checking their own watch or phone, because there is no call to prayer, no sehri call and no mosque recitation to mark the time.

In South Korea there is no arrangement for buying iftar food outside during Ramadan, so Bangladeshi expatriates prepare their own; on the weekly holidays they cook several iftar items together with friends.
On Saturdays and Sundays, the weekly holidays, various mosques in South Korea arrange iftar; expatriates also pray tarawih together with friends.

Bangladeshi community organisations in South Korea organise Quran recitation competitions, other religious programmes and iftar gatherings during Ramadan to build relations between the community and expatriates.

A Muslim in South Korea has to check food carefully for halal status: the writer says most Korean food contains pork, so even a packet of chips must be read to see whether it is halal, and restaurant meals have to be chosen with care.
Koreans are astonished when they learn that a Muslim migrant fasts from dawn to dusk in Ramadan, the writer says.
The number of local Muslims in South Korea is very small, but the number of migrant Muslims coming from Bangladesh, Pakistan, Indonesia, Egypt, Morocco and Uzbekistan is growing day by day.
According to the Korea Muslim Federation, local Korean Muslims number about 65,000, which is 0.4 percent of Korea's population, and migrant Muslims number more than 3 lakh (300,000).
facts.source_in_article: Korea Muslim Federation, cited by the writer

facts.statement: The Seoul Central Mosque and Islamic Center was built in 1969 on land given by the Korean government; the article says there are now more than three hundred small and large mosques in Korea.

named_actors.what_the_article_says: Writer of the piece; President of the Korea-Bangla Press Club.

headline_en: United States will send back illegal Bangladeshis
summary_en: Diplomatic sources told Prothom Alo that the United States, under President Trump's decision, is sending back Bangladeshis who have become undocumented, and the US embassy in Dhaka informed the Bangladesh government by diplomatic note in February 2025. Bangladesh has asked that its nationals not be returned in handcuffs, and an inter-ministerial meeting on 5 March 2025 discussed taking people back once citizenship is confirmed. No number or start date has been given by the US.

facts.statement: Under President Donald Trump's previously announced decision, the United States is sending back undocumented Bangladeshi nationals as it is doing with other countries; the US has not said how many Bangladeshis have become undocumented there or when the return process will start.
facts.source_in_article: Diplomatic sources in Dhaka and Washington, to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The US embassy in Dhaka informed the Bangladesh government in February 2025, through a diplomatic note, about sending back Bangladeshis who have become undocumented in the United States; US embassy officials also discussed it with the Foreign Ministry that month and Washington sought Dhaka's cooperation, to which the government is responding positively.

Bangladesh has requested the United States not to send Bangladeshis home in a degrading way in handcuffs; a senior Foreign Ministry official said the US administration has given assurance that it will not do so in Bangladesh's case.
facts.source_in_article: Senior Foreign Ministry official; diplomatic sources

facts.statement: An inter-ministerial meeting on bringing back Bangladeshis who have become undocumented in the United States was held at the Secretariat at noon on Wednesday 5 March 2025, chaired by Home Adviser Lt Gen (retd) Jahangir Alam Chowdhury; it discussed following the existing process, meaning people will be taken back subject to confirmation of their Bangladeshi citizenship.
facts.source_in_article: Several senior officials present at the meeting

facts.statement: Foreign Ministry officials in Dhaka and in the United States had no figure for undocumented Bangladeshis in the US, but indicated that the numbers are likely to be highest in three states: New York, New Jersey and Connecticut.

According to a BBC report cited in the article, three US government offices oversee undocumented migrants: the Office of Homeland Security, US Customs and Border Protection, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Diplomatic sources said the number of undocumented Bangladeshis in the US is not that large, so the chance that Bangladeshis will be sent back on chartered aircraft is low; they believe Bangladeshis will not be treated degradingly unless a person has a past criminal record or behaves in a hostile way over returning after becoming undocumented, but said nothing can be predicted under Trump's second term.

The article notes that the US sent undocumented people of Colombia and several other countries home in handcuffs, and that after Colombia at first refused to take its people back on military aircraft Trump announced a 25 percent tariff increase on it, after which Colombia backed down.

headline_en: 66 people including women and children rescued while being trafficked to Malaysia, five detained
summary_en: Police raided a hilltop house in Baharchhara union, Cox's Bazar (Teknaf police station) at about 4 am on 29 December 2024 and rescued 66 people, 61 of them Rohingya, who had been gathered to be trafficked to Malaysia by sea. Five alleged members of a trafficking ring were detained with rifle bullets and blades; a case was being prepared.

facts.statement: Police rescued 66 people gathered for trafficking to Malaysia by sea, and detained five members of a human-trafficking ring, from the house of Abdul Amin on a hilltop in the Moddhom Kachchhapia area of Baharchhara union, Cox's Bazar; 4 rifle bullets, 1 ramdao (machete) and 1 kirich (blade) were recovered.

Of the 66 people rescued, 18 were men, 11 women and 37 children; five were Bangladeshi citizens and the rest (the article's opening says 61 Rohingya) were residents of various Rohingya refugee camps in Cox's Bazar.

Police said the house was used as a den of the trafficking ring: people were gathered there through a broker ring with promises of a better life, jobs, and marriage for unmarried women, and the ring intended to confine them and extract more money by force on the pretext of getting them to Malaysia.
Those brought to the house from the Rohingya refugee camps had each first been charged BDT 20,000 by the trafficking ring.
The people were to be trafficked to Malaysia by sea; they were gathered in a house in Baharchhara union, Cox's Bazar (the case is with Teknaf Model Thana).
The Teknaf Model Thana officer-in-charge said a case over the incident was in process and that five days' remand would be sought for each of the detained ring members.
facts.source_in_article: Muhammad Giyas Uddin, OC, Teknaf Model Thana

headline_en: National Expatriates Day observed in Riyadh
summary_en: The Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh observed International Migrants Day and National Expatriates Day 2024 on 18 December 2024. The charge d'affaires spoke of 33 lakh Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia, upcoming events and giga projects that could expand the labour market, and urged workers to learn the language, get TTC training and the Saudi skill verification certificate, obey Saudi law, and remit through legal channels rather than hundi.

facts.statement: The charge d'affaires of the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh, S M Rakib Ullah, referred to 33 lakh (3.3 million) expatriate Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia.
facts.source_in_article: S M Rakib Ullah, Charge d'Affaires, Bangladesh Embassy Riyadh

facts.statement: The Saudi government is implementing the Skill Verification Programme in Bangladesh: under it, tests are held in Bangladesh in 33 occupations and the Saudi government issues a skills certificate.
facts.source_in_article: S M Rakib Ullah, Charge d'Affaires, Bangladesh Embassy Riyadh

facts.statement: The charge d'affaires said many expatriates get into trouble after coming to Saudi Arabia without learning the language or acquiring skills; he stressed taking training in a trade at Bangladesh's Technical Training Centres (TTC) and urged everyone to come to Saudi Arabia with a skills certificate.
facts.source_in_article: S M Rakib Ullah, Charge d'Affaires, Bangladesh Embassy Riyadh

facts.statement: He asked all Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia to obey Saudi laws and customs, to send their earnings through legal channels and not to send money through hundi.
facts.source_in_article: S M Rakib Ullah, Charge d'Affaires, Bangladesh Embassy Riyadh

facts.statement: The charge d'affaires said the prospects for expanding Bangladesh's labour market in Saudi Arabia are immense because in the coming decade Saudi Arabia will host the AFC Asian Cup in 2027, the 'winter Asian Olympics' (as printed) in 2029, World Expo in 2030 and the FIFA World Cup in 2034, and giga projects such as NEOM, Red Sea, Qiddiya, Green Riyadh, Amaala, Diriyah and Roshn are being implemented.
facts.source_in_article: S M Rakib Ullah, Charge d'Affaires, Bangladesh Embassy Riyadh

headline_en: Chance for college and university students to win money and a crest by writing an essay
summary_en: A notice that the state recruiting company BOESL is holding an essay competition for college and university students for National Expatriates Day and International Migrants Day 2024, with topics on skills and migration and on remittance. The only thing of use for a migration guide is BOESL's office address and email as printed.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, organised an essay competition for college and university students for National Expatriates Day and International Migrants Day 2024; essays had to be submitted by 3 pm on 4 December 2024, in person or scanned by email to info@boesl.gov.bd. The 3 December 2024 article describes the deadline as 'tomorrow, Wednesday (4 December)'.

The BOESL essay competition had two groups: Group Ka for class 11-12 or equivalent students, topic 'Skills and migration: Bangladesh's prospects in the global context', within 1,500 words; Group Kha for university honours/masters or equivalent students, topic 'Remittance: a sustainable driver of national economic growth', within 2,000 words. Essays had to be handwritten on one side of white A4 paper (computer composition not accepted), with half-inch margins on both sides and page numbers, and a cover page with topic, group, name, class and mobile number; no name, mobile number or coded mark anywhere in the essay itself. First, second and third in each group get cash, a crest and a certificate.

BOESL address as printed: Managing Director, Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, Probashi Kallyan Bhaban (5th floor), 71-72 Eskaton Garden, Ramna, Dhaka-1000; email info@boesl.gov.bd.

headline_en: India must understand what the people of Bangladesh want (interview with M Humayun Kabir)
summary_en: An interview with former ambassador M Humayun Kabir, president of the Bangladesh Enterprise Institute, on the strain in Bangladesh-India relations after 5 August 2024. Almost all of it is about diplomacy, but he notes that many Bangladeshi students and job seekers must travel to Delhi for third-country visas and that India has sharply limited visas since August 2024, and he credits the Chief Adviser with getting detained Bangladeshis home from the UAE and reopening the Malaysian labour market.

facts.statement: Many Bangladeshi students and job seekers have to go to Delhi to obtain visas for many third countries, former ambassador M Humayun Kabir said.
facts.source_in_article: M Humayun Kabir, former ambassador to the US, President of Bangladesh Enterprise Institute (BEI)

facts.statement: M Humayun Kabir said India gave visas easily for the previous 15 years but has very much limited visas since August 2024; he said that with Indian visas closed Bangladeshi tourists cannot go there and patients cannot get treatment as before, and that easing visas could be the first step of Indian goodwill.

A proposal was sent to Delhi to hold the foreign-secretary-level meeting (Foreign Office Consultation, FOC) in Dhaka on 10 December 2024; an Indian source said the date would be communicated once final. Kabir said that if talks are held the visa problem of Bangladeshis will be resolved (his expectation).
M Humayun Kabir said that with one telephone call by Chief Adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus it was possible to bring home more than fifty Bangladeshis who had been detained in the United Arab Emirates.
M Humayun Kabir said Bangladesh's labour market in Malaysia had been closed and that it was reopened on the Chief Adviser's initiative (his statement in the interview; no details given).

headline_en: UAE government pardons 75 more expatriate Bangladeshis
summary_en: The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry said on 29 November 2024 that the UAE government pardoned 75 more Bangladeshis detained for holding marches and protests in the UAE in July-August 2024, bringing the total released under general pardon to 188. The article recalls that 57 Bangladeshis had been sentenced to 10 years to life and that the Chief Adviser asked the UAE President by phone on 28 August 2024 to pardon them.

facts.statement: The UAE government pardoned 75 more expatriate Bangladeshis who had been detained for holding marches and protests in the UAE against the killing and repression of students and people during Bangladesh's July-August 2024 anti-discrimination movement.
facts.source_in_article: Press release sent by Shefayet Hossain, information officer, Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment

facts.statement: Including the newly released 75, the UAE has so far released a total of 188 Bangladeshis under general pardon in connection with the 2024 protests.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Chief Adviser's press secretary Shafiqul Alam said at a press conference on 3 September 2024 that the Chief Adviser spoke by telephone with the UAE President on 28 August 2024, that a large part of the call was about waiving the punishment of the 57 Bangladeshis, that the Chief Adviser requested the President to pardon the migrant workers, and that the President kept his word.
facts.source_in_article: Shafiqul Alam, Chief Adviser's press secretary

facts.statement: A UAE court had sentenced 57 Bangladeshis to prison for protesting in the UAE in solidarity with Bangladesh's quota reform movement: three to life imprisonment, 53 to 10 years and one to 11 years.

headline_en: Expatriates will be honoured like guests at the airport: Chief Adviser
summary_en: On 11 November 2024 Chief Adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus opened a dedicated Probashi Lounge for migrant workers at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka, the first of its kind there, offering rest space and subsidised food. Adviser Asif Nazrul said 100 staff sponsored by IOM have been appointed to look after migrants at the airport; Yunus also called for e-passports delivered without office visits.

facts.source_in_article: Article; Chief Adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus

facts.statement: The Probashi Lounge at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport offers Bangladeshi migrant workers a place to rest and food at affordable prices; the government will subsidise the food so that it can be served cheaply.

Law and Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Professor Asif Nazrul said 100 staff have been appointed to look after and assist expatriates at the airport, and that the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has sponsored these staff.
facts.source_in_article: Asif Nazrul, Law and Expatriates' Welfare Adviser

facts.statement: Fatima Nusrat Ghazzali, deputy chief of the IOM mission in Bangladesh, said the United Nations sponsored the lounge to assist Bangladeshi migrant workers.
facts.source_in_article: Fatima Nusrat Ghazzali, Deputy Chief of Mission, IOM Bangladesh

facts.statement: The Chief Adviser said expatriates should now be given e-passports, that printed passports are not needed, and that arrangements must be made so the passport comes on the phone and people do not have to go to an office (stated as something that must be done, not as an existing service).

The Chief Adviser said expatriates do not get proper respect and service at the airport, that the government has taken steps so they are treated like guests, that the lounge is the first step and more measures are hoped for; he also said expatriates' hard-earned money is being laundered abroad by others and the country's money must stay in the country.

headline_en: Bangladeshi killed in air strike in Lebanese capital Beirut
summary_en: The Bangladesh Embassy in Beirut confirmed that expatriate Mohammad Nizam of Kasba, Brahmanbaria, was killed in an air strike in Beirut's Hazmieh area on 2 November 2024 while on his way to work. His wife is in Lebanon, and she was told the body cannot be sent to Bangladesh because there are no flights during the war.

facts.statement: Expatriate Bangladeshi Mohammad Nizam was killed on the spot in an air strike in the Hazmieh area of Beirut on Saturday 2 November 2024 at 3:23 pm local time, while at a coffee shop on his way to his workplace.

The dead man, Mohammad Nizam, was aged 31 years 11 months according to his passport; his father is Mohammad Abdul Quddus, mother Mosammat Anwara Begum, and his home is in the Kharera area of Kasba upazila, Brahmanbaria district.
Nizam's wife is in Lebanon and the embassy is in contact with her; she has been told that because there are no flights in the war situation it will not be possible to send Nizam's body to Bangladesh.

Israel had been striking Lebanon from time to time since the Gaza war began on 7 October 2023, but for about a month before early November 2024 it carried out continuous heavy strikes against Hezbollah as well as a ground operation.
Citing Lebanon's health ministry, Al Jazeera reported that at least 2,867 people have been killed and 13,047 injured in Israeli attacks in Lebanon since 7 October 2023.

headline_en: 52 Lebanon expatriates returning home tonight
summary_en: A sixth group of 52 Bangladeshis who applied to the embassy in Beirut for voluntary return because of the war left Beirut for Dhaka via Dubai on 31 October 2024. The article lists the five earlier groups (216 people) and says about 1,800 of an estimated 70,000 to 100,000 Bangladeshis in Lebanon have expressed interest in returning.

facts.statement: Because of the ongoing war, 52 Bangladeshi expatriates left Beirut Rafic Hariri International Airport for Dhaka via Dubai on Thursday 31 October 2024; their aircraft was due to land at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport at about 11 pm. They are the sixth group of Bangladeshis who applied to the Bangladesh Embassy in Beirut to return home voluntarily.

headline_en: Why are Bangladeshis being rounded up in the Maldives (reader's letter)
summary_en: A letter from a Bangladeshi worker in the Maldives says continuous round-ups are under way, with people whose visas are not in order taken even from houses and those with valid visas also harassed, and claims Bangladeshis are being singled out. He describes the cost of fixing and keeping a visa, visas cancelled while on leave, unpaid wages from companies and contractors, and workers brought in and left on the street.

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi worker in the Maldives writes that continuous round-ups are going on: people whose visas are not in order are now being picked up not only on the streets but from houses, and those whose visas are in order are also being harassed.
facts.source_in_article: Sheikh Sajib Ahmed, Maldives expatriate (letter writer)

facts.statement: The letter writer alleges that only Bangladeshis are being sought out and detained while people of other countries working illegally are not; he says other nationalities are detained when there is a complaint of doing business illegally, that some Bangladeshis are also involved in illegal business, and that ordinary employees are picked up when authorities come for them.

According to the letter, many Bangladeshi workers in the Maldives have spent two lakh taka to get their visa regularised, and have to pay a lot of money every year to keep the visa valid; even after paying they face harassment.
The letter says that when a worker goes home on leave, some (employers or sponsors, not specified) cancel the worker's visa.
The authorities tell workers to work at their own (sponsoring) company, the letter says; the writer responds that workers cannot find such companies and that some companies do not pay wages properly.

The letter says some companies in the Maldives do not pay wages properly, contractors also end up withholding wages, and that earlier workers were brought in and left on the street; the writer sees no good companies for newly arriving workers.
The letter writer believes the round-ups are happening because new workers will be brought from Bangladesh (his claim).
The writer predicts that those who come on company visas will face low pay and long duty hours and will run away from the company and become undocumented.
The letter says many Bangladeshi expatriates in the Maldives are being left destitute after falling into the hands of brokers.

facts.statement: According to the editorial, 20 to 22 lakh young people join Bangladesh's labour market every year; at most 12 to 13 lakh find work in the domestic market (about 85 percent of them in minimum-wage informal work), and 8 to 9 lakh people go abroad each year; the rest have no work opportunity.

summary_en: Human Rights Watch, in a report published on its website on 24 July 2024, called the conviction of 57 Bangladeshis in the UAE unfair after they protested on 19 July 2024 in support of Bangladesh's quota reform movement. An Abu Dhabi court sentenced them to 10 years to life after a one-day hearing, with deportation after the sentence; HRW notes that protests and assemblies are completely banned under the UAE penal code.

facts.statement: According to Human Rights Watch, protests in support of Bangladesh's quota movement took place in various parts of the UAE on 19 July 2024, mostly by Bangladeshis, and on 21 July 2024 a court sentenced 57 Bangladeshi protesters to prison terms from 10 years to life (the article describes 21 July as 'one day later').
facts.source_in_article: Human Rights Watch report published 24 July 2024

facts.statement: Citing the UAE state news agency, HRW said the Abu Dhabi court sentenced 53 Bangladeshis to 10 years, 1 to 11 years and 3 to life imprisonment, and ordered that they be deported to their country after completing the sentences; the sentences came after only one day of hearing.
facts.source_in_article: UAE state news agency via Human Rights Watch

facts.statement: HRW's report says there are strict restrictions on freedom of expression and assembly in the UAE and that under the country's penal code protests and gatherings are completely banned.

headline_en: 57 Bangladeshis jailed for protesting in the Emirates
summary_en: A UAE court sentenced 57 Bangladeshis to prison (three to life, 53 to 10 years, one to 11 years) for protesting in the UAE on 19 July 2024 in solidarity with Bangladesh's quota reform movement, with deportation after the sentences, the state news agency WAM reported on 22 July 2024. The Bangladesh embassy in Abu Dhabi and consulate in Dubai had warned on 20 July that gatherings, slogans and posting such content online without permission are banned and can lead to visa cancellation, jail, fines, deportation or an entry ban.

facts.statement: A UAE court sentenced 57 Bangladeshis to prison for protesting in the UAE in solidarity with Bangladesh's quota reform movement: three to life, 53 to 10 years and one to 11 years; the state news agency WAM said they would be deported to their country after serving the sentences.

WAM reported that the convicted people protested against their own country's government; a witness confirmed they had organised large protests on several roads in the UAE against a decision of the Bangladesh government. Khaleej Times reported the protest took place on Friday 19 July 2024.
Any kind of protest without permission is banned in the United Arab Emirates.

The Bangladesh Embassy in Abu Dhabi and the Bangladesh Consulate General in Dubai stated that under UAE law it is prohibited to hold any meeting or gathering or chant slogans without prior permission of the proper authorities, and completely prohibited to do anything that may create unrest, panic or confusion among the public, to spread rumours or propaganda, or to record such statements, photos or videos and publish them on social media.

facts.statement: The missions' statement warned that anyone doing these things may face severe punishment: their visa may be cancelled, they may be jailed or fined, deported from the Emirates, or banned from entering the Emirates in future; it asked all Bangladeshis living in the UAE to obey local laws and regulations.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Embassy Abu Dhabi and Consulate General Dubai statement

facts.statement: In a separate statement on Monday 22 July 2024 the Bangladesh Embassy in Abu Dhabi said more than 10 lakh (1 million) Bangladeshis live in the Emirates and that the handful who acted illegally do not represent Bangladesh.

headline_en: One in three who returned from abroad in five years is from Chattogram
summary_en: The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics' Socio-Economic and Demographic Survey 2023, published in the first week of June 2024, breaks down migrants who returned permanently in the past five years by home division, country returned from, reason for return and education. Chattogram division accounts for 36.36 percent, Saudi Arabia for 38.37 percent of returns, and the top stated reasons are voluntary return and visa expiry. BMET outflow figures are also given.

facts.statement: Of expatriates who returned permanently to Bangladesh in the past five years, 36.36 percent are from Chattogram division, 35.25 percent Dhaka, 7.75 percent Khulna, 6.93 percent Sylhet, 6.69 percent Rajshahi, 2.95 percent Mymensingh, 2.60 percent Barishal and 1.64 percent Rangpur (the lowest).

Of permanently returned migrants, 38.37 percent came back from Saudi Arabia, 14 percent from the United Arab Emirates, 13.15 percent from Malaysia, 9.20 percent from Oman, 5.67 percent from Qatar, 4.37 percent from Kuwait and 3.12 percent from Singapore; Bahrain, Maldives, Lebanon, Iraq, Brunei Darussalam and South Africa are also on the list.

Reasons for permanent return among returnees: 17.28 percent returned voluntarily, 12.80 percent because the visa expired, 11.67 percent 'by the relevant authority' (as printed), 9.24 percent for health reasons, 9.21 percent because of Covid, 7.96 percent to live with family and 7.18 percent because they lost their job.

Education of permanently returned migrants: 42.28 percent studied class five to eight, 12.32 percent passed SSC or equivalent, 10.78 percent studied class one to four, 5.10 percent passed HSC or equivalent, and 25.38 percent never attended an educational institution.
According to BMET, more than 10 lakh workers went abroad in a year for the first time in 2017; more than 11 lakh 35 thousand went in 2022; and a record of more than 13 lakh went in 2023.

facts.statement: The Oman embassy in Dhaka said that from now on the embassy, in coordination with Oman police, will receive visa applications and related documents for the reopened categories and act according to the rules.
In October 2023 the Royal Oman Police imposed a temporary ban on all types of visa for Bangladeshi nationals other than government officials, in order to overhaul Oman's immigration policy.

The ban on worker (labour) visas for Bangladeshis in Oman had not been lifted as of 12 June 2024; Bangladesh's Foreign Ministry said it is working with the Omani authorities to get the worker-visa ban withdrawn.

headline_en: Highest remittance in four years came in May
summary_en: Remittances through banking channels reached USD 225 crore (2.25 billion) in May 2024, the highest in about 46 months and the second highest ever, after the central bank raised the official dollar rate by 7 taka to 117 taka. The article gives fiscal-year totals, the rate banks pay exchange houses, and reserve figures, and quotes bankers that hundi and money laundering must be curbed.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 225 crore in remittances through banking channels in May 2024, the highest in about four years (46 months) and the second highest ever; the highest single month was USD 260 crore in July 2020.
In May 2024 Bangladesh Bank raised the official price of the US dollar in one jump by 7 taka, fixing it at 117 taka; the article says the rise in the dollar's price increased remittance inflow.
Banks were buying remittances from foreign exchange houses at rates of up to 118 taka 30 paisa per US dollar.

According to Bangladesh Bank, remittances in the first 11 months of fiscal year 2023-24 were USD 2,137 crore, USD 196 crore or 10 percent more than the USD 1,941 crore of the same period a year earlier; the whole previous fiscal year brought USD 2,161 crore.
Expatriates sent USD 204 crore through banking channels in April 2024, against USD 169 crore in the same month a year earlier; remittances usually rise before Eid every year.

Bangladesh Bank's foreign exchange reserves fell to USD 18.72 billion on 29 May 2024, from USD 19.96 billion in April 2024 and USD 21.87 billion at the end of December 2023; the record was USD 48 billion in August 2021.
Bankers said that to raise remittances through banking channels strict action against money laundering and hundi is needed, and that merely raising the dollar price pushes up import costs.

headline_en: Thousands crowd Dhaka airport without air tickets to go to Malaysia
summary_en: On 31 May 2024, the last day Malaysia would admit approved Bangladeshi workers, thousands waited at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport without air tickets after paying recruiting firms five to seven lakh taka each. Named workers had waited two to three days while their agencies stopped answering calls; the airport said extra flights were being arranged.

facts.statement: In March 2024 Malaysia said it would not take workers for the time being, and that those who had already received approval and visas must enter Malaysia by 31 May 2024 (a Friday).
Malaysia's labour market reopened to Bangladeshis in 2022 after being closed for four years over irregularities in sending workers through a ring (syndicate); a ring was then formed again.

Thousands of people crowded Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, on 31 May 2024 hoping to fly to Malaysia, many without air tickets, because they had paid recruiting agencies and believed that after that day Malaysia would take no more workers from Bangladesh.

At least 10 more passengers waiting at the airport told Prothom Alo they had paid the firms five to seven lakh taka each to go to Malaysia; some doubted whether the companies would refund the money if they could not go, and they demanded the government act to extend the deadline.

Habibur Rahman of Natore deposited six and a half lakh taka with a firm (not named) to go to Malaysia, raised by mortgaging land and taking a bank loan; company people brought him to the airport three days earlier, he had no ticket as of 5 pm on 31 May 2024, and they stopped answering his calls; someone he sent to the company's office was told to wait.

Rubel Mia of Narsingdi paid six lakh taka to a firm named Ahad Enterprise to go to Malaysia as a construction worker; he had waited two days at Dhaka airport with a brother without getting a ticket, and when he called the company people said they would arrange it.

The executive director of the airport, Kamrul Islam, said there had been heavy pressure of Malaysia-bound passengers for two days and that extra flights were being arranged in addition to regular flights to handle it.

headline_en: Proposal to start online classes for Bangladeshi students in Kyrgyzstan
summary_en: After recent incidents in Bishkek (a linked headline refers to attacks on foreigners), Bangladesh's ambassador to Kyrgyzstan, resident in Tashkent, met the Kyrgyz deputy education minister on 22 May 2024 and asked that Bangladeshi students be allowed online classes for the next few months. The deputy minister said government and universities are working on foreign students' safety and that he would consider the request positively.

facts.statement: Bangladesh's ambassador to the Kyrgyz Republic, Mohammad Monirul Islam (resident in Tashkent, Uzbekistan), met Kyrgyz deputy education minister Rasul Avazbek uulu in Bishkek on Wednesday 22 May 2024 and, citing recent incidents in Bishkek, asked him to ensure a safe environment for Bangladeshi students studying at universities in Kyrgyzstan.

The ambassador requested that Bangladeshi students be given the option, according to their needs, of attending classes online for the next few months; the deputy minister assured him he would consider online classes positively.

facts.statement: The Kyrgyz deputy education minister said that not only government authorities but also university administrations are working sincerely to ensure the safety of foreign students including Bangladeshis; he also expressed interest in concluding a memorandum of understanding on education cooperation with Bangladesh's relevant ministry.

facts.statement: The ambassador discussed academic activities, security, accommodation, transport and food with rectors, vice rectors and deans of universities where Bangladeshi students study, and was told the universities are active in ensuring the students' safety and welfare.
Bangladesh's embassy covering Kyrgyzstan is in Tashkent, Uzbekistan: the ambassador to the Kyrgyz Republic is resident in Tashkent.

Linked headlines inside the article say foreigners were attacked in Kyrgyzstan, Bangladeshi students were in fear, and Pakistan took 140 of its students home (headlines only; no detail in this article).

headline_en: UK will quickly send back illegal Bangladeshis
summary_en: The UK and Bangladesh agreed in London in the week of 17 May 2024, at the first joint working group on home affairs, on a fast-track arrangement to return failed asylum seekers, foreign offenders and visa overstayers to Bangladesh, removing mandatory interviews where evidence is strong. About 11,000 Bangladeshis who entered on student, visit or work visas claimed asylum last year and 95 percent were refused.

facts.statement: The United Kingdom made a new agreement with Bangladesh under which people whose asylum claims have been rejected, foreign criminals and people whose visas have expired will be returned to Bangladesh by a 'fast-track' process.
The UK-Bangladesh agreement eases returns by allowing people to be sent back without a mandatory interview in cases where there is strong evidence for removing them.

About 11,000 Bangladeshis who came to the UK on student, visit or work visas applied for asylum last year in order to stay permanently; UK immigration authorities rejected 95 percent of these applications, and the rejected applicants will now be returned under the new agreement.

The agreement was reached at the first UK-Bangladesh joint working group on home affairs, held in London; the group also committed to continuing to facilitate legal migration through existing visa routes, tackling illegal migration, stronger information sharing and understanding each other's approaches to serious organised crime.
UK minister for illegal migration Michael Tomlinson said speeding up removals is an important part of the plan to stop people coming and staying illegally, and called Bangladesh a valued partner.

headline_en: Jordan to take women workers, with medical care and air fare provided
summary_en: BOESL published a notice to recruit 150 women machine operators for Sidney Apparels LLC, a textile company in Jordan, by walk-in interview on 15 March 2024 at the Sheikh Fazilatunnesa Mujib Mohila TTC in Mirpur. Basic pay is BDT 19,184 a month on a three-year renewable contract with free accommodation, food, primary medical care and air fare; selected workers pay only a BDT 1,000 medical fee and BDT 220 fingerprint fee.

facts.statement: Through the state company Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), 150 women workers are to be recruited as machine operators for Sidney Apparels LLC (শিডনি অ্যাপারেলস এলএলসি), a textile/garment company in Jordan, by direct interview.

Eligibility for the BOESL Jordan machine-operator recruitment: experience in the relevant work and age between 20 and 35; priority for Sudan-returned workers on the basis of qualification and skill in the work, and for certificate holders trained in the garments trade at BMET-run technical training centres. Anyone with a case against them in Bangladesh or Jordan is ineligible.
The monthly basic salary for women machine operators at Sidney Apparels LLC in Jordan via BOESL is BDT 19,184; duty is 8 hours a day, 6 days a week, with overtime available.

The Jordan job contract is for three years and renewable; the employer provides accommodation, food, primary medical care and transport costs, pays the air fare for joining, and pays the return air fare after three years of satisfactory service; other terms follow Jordan's labour law.
Selected workers for the BOESL Jordan recruitment have to pay a medical fee of BDT 1,000 and a fingerprint fee of BDT 220; the notice says there is no other cost.

Interested candidates were to attend the interview at 8 am on 15 March 2024 at the Sheikh Fazilatunnesa Mujib Mohila Technical Training Centre, Mirpur (Dhaka), bringing: four passport-size colour photographs, the original passport, one colour and four black-and-white photocopies of the passport's photo page, current office ID card or attendance card, and educational/experience certificates if any.
For information on the BOESL Jordan recruitment the notice gives telephone numbers 02-48319125 and 02-48317515.

summary_en: BOESL announced recruitment of 200 women workers for Eurotex Textile Company in Turkey: 100 texturising workers and 100 spinning, dyeing and garment workers, on two-year renewable contracts with accommodation, food at work and air fare paid by the company. Applicants needed SSC, height of at least 5 ft 3 in and spoken English; applications closed 20 February 2024 and selected workers pay BOESL BDT 56,350 by pay order. facts.statement: Under the management of the state company BOESL, 200 women workers are to be recruited for Eurotex Textile Company (ইউরোটেক্স টেক্সটাইল কোম্পানি) in Turkey: 100 as 'texturising worker' (printed as টেক্সটার্সিং ওয়ার্কার) and 100 as spinning, dyeing and garment workers.
Eligibility for the BOESL Turkey recruitment: at least SSC or equivalent, height at least 5 feet 3 inches, proficient in spoken English, and age between 18 and 35.
The article's headline gives the salary for the Turkey jobs as BDT 51,000; the body of the article does not state a salary figure.

Terms for the Turkey jobs: labour contract of two years, renewable; probation of three months; 8 hours' duty a day; overtime under Turkey's labour law; one weekly day off; accommodation borne by the company; food provided by the company while at work; air fare paid by the company.

Candidates had to apply through BOESL's link with a CV in English, educational qualifications, experience and other information by 20 February 2024; BOESL screens applicants and prepares a preliminary list, and final selection is by interview with the company's representative.
Finally selected workers for Turkey must deposit a pay order with BOESL for a total of BDT 56,350, covering BOESL's service charge and incidental expenses.

headline_en: Bodies of five Naogaon men killed in Saudi Arabia fire return home after three months
summary_en: The bodies of seven Bangladeshi workers, five from Naogaon and two from Natore, arrived in Dhaka on 31 October 2026, 2 months 22 days after a fire at a sofa factory in Riyadh on 9 August 2026 killed 16 Bangladeshis; these seven had to be identified by DNA testing. Families describe loans of BDT 5.7 to 7 lakh taken to migrate, one worker went a year without an iqama, and the Atrai UNO said each family will get BDT 35,000 for burial now and a BDT 3 lakh grant after three months.

facts.statement: Sixteen Bangladeshi workers were killed in a fire at a sofa-making factory in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on 9 August (2026).

Of the 16 Bangladeshis killed in the Riyadh sofa factory fire, nine bodies were sent home on 27 August; the remaining seven, whose bodies were disfigured by burning, were identified by DNA testing and reached Bangladesh on 31 October 2026, 2 months 22 days after the fire.

The flight carrying the seven bodies, a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight, landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at about 8:30 am on Saturday 31 October 2026; after the necessary airport procedures, officials of the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry handed the bodies to relatives, who took them to Naogaon and Natore.

The seven identified by DNA were, from Naogaon: Md. Shahin of Par Naogaon, Naogaon municipality; Hasibul Hasan of Dubai village, Atrai upazila; Minhaz Pramanik of Moddhoboalia village, Atrai; Masidul Sardar of Madhabpur village; and Sagor Ali of Sadhonnagar village; and from Naldanga upazila, Natore: Mohammad Shamim of Dighirpar village and Sabbir Hossain of Khajura village.
The Atrai upazila nirbahi officer said 11 people from Atrai upazila (Naogaon) died in the Saudi fire; seven of their bodies came in the first round on 27 August and four in this round.
The Atrai UNO said each family of the dead will for now be given BDT 35,000 for burial of the body, and after three months each affected family will be given a grant of BDT 3 lakh.

Shahin (printed both as শাহিন and শাহীন) of Par Naogaon, a father of two and his mother's only child, went to Saudi Arabia in April 2026 on borrowed money; his mother Nargis Begum said he took a loan of BDT 5 lakh 70 thousand from a samity (সমিতি, a society; not further identified) to go. He found work and was killed in the factory fire three months after arriving.
facts.source_in_article: Nargis Begum, mother of Shahin; article

facts.statement: Akkas Pramanik said he sent his son Minhaz Pramanik of Moddhoboalia, Atrai, to Saudi Arabia a year ago by borrowing seven lakh taka, through a broker ring.

Minhaz Pramanik, who went to Saudi Arabia through a broker ring, did not get an iqama (residence permit) even in one year; he got work at a sofa factory in Riyadh four months before his death and had sent some money home after that. His father is now worried about how to repay the loan.
